verdicts.why: Names a male under someone's command or employ; the rank is the meaning, and the word takes no side on him.
A plain count noun for a member of a military force, as in 'the regiment lost forty men', with no attitude attached.
A game piece is an object; the word describes it and nothing more.
A dated but plain word for a valet or personal servant; it states the relation without approving or belittling him.
Receiving news or a message is described flatly; the sentences show it used for welcome and unwelcome news alike.
A technical legal sense for a court examining a case; purely procedural, no judgement of anyone.
In this sense a friend is one who backs a cause or team; the favourable disposition is the meaning itself, not an attitude the speaker adds beyond it.
A conventional title of address for a mother superior; respectful by convention, not a judgement chosen over a plainer word.
A technical name for the vinegar culture; the substance may be slimy but the word simply names it.
The polite formula ('with pleasure', 'my pleasure') expresses courtesy toward the hearer; it passes no judgement on any referent.
A mild, somewhat delicate word for sexual gratification, but delicacy is not judgement; it neither disapproves of nor leers at what it names.
The faculty of concentrating is named neutrally; the sentences use it for both its presence and its want without the word itself taking a side.
The work of attending to or treating someone is described plainly, as in medical attention.
A drill posture with a fixed technical name; there is nothing to judge.
Covering a distance on foot is the plainest possible motion verb; the sentences show it used with no colouring at all.
Causing someone or an animal to walk, as in walking a dog or walking a guest to the door, describes the act without attitude.

Being in company or association with someone, as in 'walk with God', names the relation without approving or disparaging it.
A gait term for a horse or rider moving at a walk; purely descriptive of pace.
A baseball term for reaching first base on balls; a rule outcome with no evaluative charge.
The pitcher's side of the same baseball outcome; technical and neutral.

Spelling out the letters of a word is a mechanical act named plainly.
